notes:
I've put together notes on all 13 verses. A few things you should know first:

- **Missing sources.** I couldn't read Spurgeon's page in full, so his points come only from search snippets. I didn't reach preceptaustin, Lutheran or Orthodox sites, or the full NET Bible notes beyond verses 1–3.
- **No real Protestant split.** I found no verse where Protestant traditions clearly disagree. Below I flag the closest thing to a difference, which is a matter of emphasis.
- **No popular modern teaching.** None of the pages I read discussed prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm, so that section is left out.
- **Uncited pages.** Points from the full Pulpit Commentary page (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html) and the full Enduring Word page (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/) appear without citation markers because of how those pages loaded. Their URLs are given, and what I report comes from my reading of them.

---

## Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1 (title).**
- Enduring Word (Guzik) links the title to 1 Samuel 21:10–15. It says the tune was probably the melody, though some connect it with the theme: a dove in trouble even as David was in trouble. He reads Miktam as most likely meaning golden, though others think it is related to a word meaning to cover, implying necessary secrecy in a time of crisis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- Guzik also notes that David asks for mercy rather than relying on what he deserves. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- The Pulpit Commentary says "swallow me up" literally means "pants after me," like a beast after its prey. It notes the contrast between frail "man" (enosh) and the mighty God (Elohim), and takes the "silent dove" to be David himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html
- Clarke (Wesleyan) says David expected little mercy from man, so he looked to God for it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-56.html

**v. 2.**
- The Pulpit Commentary says "mine enemies" literally means "my watchers," which would suit a prisoner. It adds that the old rendering "O Most High" is now generally dropped in favour of "proudly." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html
- Guzik keeps "Most High" and draws a lesson about seeking the high ground. He also mentions Clarke's view that the word means "from on high," not a title for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/

**v. 3.**
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon that fear and faith aren't opposites—David admits he is afraid, yet declares he will trust in God at the same moment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- The Pulpit Commentary reads the verse as "the day when I am afraid": when fear creeps in, David chooses to trust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

**v. 4.**
- Matthew Henry says David praises God's word as well as his works: I will give him thanks for a promise, though not yet performed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/psalms/56.htm
- Barnes says God's "word," meaning his gracious promise, is the special thing David praises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-4.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown takes "flesh" as a picture of human frailty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the verse the psalm's refrain and keynote, and calls it the true martyr spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

**vv. 5–6.**
- Guzik says the attacks were devious as well as violent. He quotes Spurgeon that such enemies "put our language on the rack." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the enemies twisted David's words to turn King Achish against him. It reads v. 6 as "they set an ambush," with even the great men stooping to spy on his steps. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

**v. 7.**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the question to mean: will they escape God's judgement by their wickedness? Certainly not. It takes "the peoples" to mean the heathen, including the men of Gath. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html
- Guzik calls this an appeal to God's justice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/

**v. 8.**
- **Wanderings.** The Pulpit Commentary takes these as David's moves from city to cave to wilderness.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-8.htm
- Ellicott instead reads the singular "wandering" as "mental restlessness," the "tossings to and fro of the mind." He notes a play of words in the original of "bottle," and "wandering." https://biblehub.com/psalms/56-8.htm
- **The bottle.** Commentators disagree about whether Roman "tear bottles" lie behind the image:
  - Clarke and Gill see an allusion to them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-8.html
  - Spurgeon denies it. He says the picture is a stronger one: such floods of tears had David wept that a leathern bottle would scarce hold them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps056.cfm
  - Ellicott also warns against assuming tear bottles. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-8.htm
- **The book.** Calvin reads "are they not in your book?" as a statement that David already had what he asked for. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-8.html
- Matthew Henry says God has a bottle and a book for his people's tears, both those for their sins and those for their afflictions. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-8.html
- Gill stresses that the tears are kept, but not to make atonement for sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-8.html
- Got Questions sums up the point: The idea behind the keeping of "tears in a bottle" is remembrance. https://www.gotquestions.org/tears-in-a-bottle.html

**v. 9.**
- Guzik says David's wanderings and tears did not mean God was against him. He cites Kidner that Paul echoes this verse in Romans 8:31. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- The Pulpit Commentary says "when I cry" literally means "in the day that I call." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

**vv. 10–11.**
- Guzik says this is the second and third time David praises God's word, so he is preaching confidence to himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- The Pulpit Commentary says the refrain is not empty repetition. Verse 10 adds the covenant name "the LORD," and v. 11's "man" means man at his strongest, where v. 4 had "flesh," man at his weakest. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

**v. 12.**
- The Pulpit Commentary says David made vows (promised thank offerings) while in danger and now considers them due. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html
- Guzik cites Kidner that "thank offerings" can mean literal sacrifices or songs of gratitude. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- Bible.org's notes say that In this request he made some kind of a vow. God did save him, now he must fulfill his vow. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21555

**v. 13.**
- Barnes takes "soul" to mean David's life. He notes that Scripture pictures the grave as darkness and this world as light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-13.htm
- Calvin says "before God" marks the righteous, who make God the aim of their lives. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-13.html
- Gill and Maclaren connect the verse with Jesus' "light of life" (John 8:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-13.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch say the "light of life" is not exclusively the sun-light of this present life. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/56-13.htm

## Where Protestant traditions differ

I found no clear disagreement between traditions on this psalm. The closest is a difference in emphasis:

- **v. 12 (Wesleyan).** Clarke turns the vows into a personal challenge about the reader's own baptismal vows: renouncing the devil, keeping God's commandments and walking before him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-56/
- **v. 13 (Wesleyan).** Clarke reads deliverance as My life from the grave, and my soul from endless perdition. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/56-13.html
- **v. 13 (Pulpit homiletics).** One sermon asks whether a believer who has been saved can fall away. Its answer: he would fall if left to himself, but Christ will not forsake a soul that trusts him (citing John 10:28–30). That leans towards the Reformed view of perseverance, but no Arminian reply to this point appeared in what I read. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html

## Other views

**Modern scholarship and the Hebrew text**
- **v. 1 (title).** The NET notes say the tune title literally means "silent dove, distant ones." It may refer to a musical style, a tune title or an instrument. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/xml/passage.php?passage=Psa+56%3A1-3
- **v. 4.** Ellicott says the text may be corrupt, because the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "my words." He suggests "I praise God with my word." https://biblehub.com/psalms/56-4.htm
- **v. 7.** An NIV footnote says the Hebrew text lacks the "do not" that the NIV adds. https://www.blueletterbible.org/niv/psa/56/1/s_534001
- **v. 10.** Cheyne, quoted in the Pulpit Commentary, calls "In the LORD..." "a feeble Jehovistic interpolation, which interrupts the refrain." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-56.html
- **v. 13.** The Revised Version and Cheyne read "hast thou not delivered," so David speaks of the rescue as already done. https://biblehub.com/psalms/56-13.htm

**Catholic (Augustine, who comments on the Latin text, so the wording differs from the BSB)**
All points below are from https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801056.htm
- **Title.** Gath stands for "strangers": All they that refuse Christ for King become strangers.
- **v. 1.** Augustine says to watch for two enemies, man whom we see and the devil whom we don't. Being trodden down is like being a grape trodden to make wine.
- **v. 6.** He reads the lurking enemies as false brethren inside the Church, with Judas as the pattern.
- **v. 7.** His Latin reads "For nothing You shall save them." He takes it as saving with not any merits of their going before, by free grace, and urges prayer for enemies.
- **v. 9.** He says enemies being turned back is for their own good.

If you need them, I can do another pass for NET notes on verses 4–13, preceptaustin, and Lutheran or Orthodox sources.
